clue.text: Imposing women arrange bets

blocks.note: to do a room, or someone's hair, is to arrange it
a wager is a bet, the older and grander word for it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Imposing' looks like an instruction — to impose is to place one thing upon another — and it is nothing of the kind. It is half the definition, doing plain descriptive work.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow who keeps her late husband's title, and the word carries exactly the grand, formidable bearing 'imposing' describes.

clue.text: Particular canine abandoned by waterway

indicators.note: To be abandoned by someone is to be left without them, so the longer word has to be read minus that letter.

blocks.note: a canal is a waterway cut by hand rather than one a river made
a dentist marks the canine tooth C on a chart, and that C is what walks out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Canine' puts a dog on the towpath, which is the whole misdirection: it is the tooth, and the tooth is written as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Anal' is short for anal-retentive, so it means obsessively fussy over detail — the pointed sense of 'particular' rather than the neutral one.

clue.text: Car rentals regularly in competition

indicators.note: At regular intervals means every second letter of the word beside it, not the whole of it.
'in' is literal placement: the letters it introduces land inside the following word rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: a bee is a competition — a spelling bee, a quilting bee
every other letter of rEnTaLs: the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Car rentals' reads as one phrase at the hire desk, which is where the misdirection lives: the definition stops dead after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: The VW Beetle was named for its domed, insect-shaped shell, so 'Car' reaches the answer through one very famous model.

clue.text: Derisive remark about my Picasso?

blocks.note: a jeer is a taunt shouted at somebody
'my!' and 'well!' are the same mild exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody sneering at a painting, so Pablo is the Picasso you reach for. The clue wants his daughter, who works in a different material.
explanation.definitionFit: Paloma Picasso has designed jewellery for Tiffany for decades, so the surname names a trade through one practitioner — which the question mark admits.

clue.text: Fruit recipe stopping tennis ace going bananas

definitions.note: 'Fruit' is a mass noun with no -s of its own, so it defines a plural answer without ever agreeing with it in number.

indicators.note: To stop a gap is to plug it, so this letter is wedged into the middle rather than added at either end.
Anything going bananas has lost all order, and letters that lose their order come back in a new one.

blocks.note: the nine letters of those two words, handed back in another order
R is the short form of recipe, the word that once headed a prescription

explanation.walkthrough: Half the vocabulary here belongs in a fruit salad, and that is the joke: 'bananas' is the one fruit word that turns out to be an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned variety of peach, so the definition is simply the plain category the answer sits in.

clue.text: Top ambassador interrupting ball

indicators.note: An interruption breaks into something already under way, so these letters land in the middle of the word rather than after it.

blocks.note: a bead is a small ball, the kind threaded on a string
an ambassador is His or Her Excellency, HE in diplomatic address

explanation.walkthrough: 'Top ambassador' reads as one phrase about a senior diplomat. 'Top' is standing alone, and it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To top something is to cut its top off — the gardener's word and the executioner's — which is exactly the operation the answer names.

clue.text: Wrestler’s trick with bad acne

indicators.note: 'bad' here means spoiled, gone off, and letters that have gone off no longer sit in the order they were given.

blocks.note: in the slang of sex work a client is a trick, and the same client is a john
the four letters of ACNE, returned in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a teenager's skin complaint, and nothing in it points at a person until 'trick' is heard as a noun from another world entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cena is a WWE wrestler turned film actor, so the definition names the answer by the trade he made his name in.

clue.text: Means business

blocks.note: the philosopher's sense: the capacity to act, the power by which a thing gets done
a firm that acts for its clients — an advertising one, an estate one, a recruitment one

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no wordplay whatever. 'Means business' is an idiom about determination, and reading it as one phrase is exactly what stops you splitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the power to act, the means by which something happens; the other is the firm that acts on a client's behalf.

clue.text: Small opening in Gogglebox you once rejected

indicators.note: To reject something is to throw it back, and a word thrown back is read the other way round.

blocks.note: the gogglebox is British slang for the television set, the tele
'ye' is the old form of 'you', the one Chaucer's readers used

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Gogglebox the television programme, people filmed watching television, while the letters need the older slang for the set in the corner.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelet is the small ringed hole punched in a shoe or a sail for a lace or a rope to pass through.

clue.text: Sample from Lulu apparently repulsed my colleague

indicators.note: A sample is a piece taken out of something larger, so the letters are lifted from within the words that follow.
To repulse is to drive back, so the letters picked out run in the opposite direction.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sample from Lulu' reads as a record credit, which is where the eye goes. 'My colleague' means a fellow Guardian setter, so the definition wants a person rather than a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul is one of the Guardian's regular cryptic setters, so 'my colleague' identifies the answer as a name on the same rota as Brockwell.

clue.text: Musicians performing late in ancient city

indicators.note: To perform a piece is to give your own arrangement of it, so the word beside this comes out arranged differently.
'in' is doing literal work.

blocks.note: Thebes, the great city of ancient Egypt on the Nile
the four letters of LATE, shuffled before they go in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Musicians performing late' is a complete picture of a band on after midnight, and every word of it turns out to be doing a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Musicians' is a plain category label, and the plural covers a four-man group whose name carries its own definite article.

clue.text: Stuff clinging to the back of Pete Best?

indicators.note: Something clinging to an object has its arms all the way round it, so one word closes over the letter that follows.

blocks.note: to stuff yourself and to gorge are the same greedy verb
the last letter of PetE

explanation.walkthrough: Pete Best reads as one name, the drummer the band let go, and the clue takes him apart: Pete supplies a letter, and Best is the definition — George Best the footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: George Best was Manchester United's Northern Irish winger, so 'Best?' reaches a first name through one famous bearer of the surname.

clue.text: One who may charge money around statue

blocks.note: rhino is old British slang for cash
c. for circa, the letter written in front of an approximate date
the winged archer above Piccadilly Circus, London's best-known statue

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'around': it looks like an instruction to wrap one piece about another, and it pays out a single letter instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhinoceros charges — lowers its horn and runs at you — while the billing sense of 'charge' belongs entirely to the surface.

clue.text: Militant going into business with John Denver here

indicators.note: To go into a thing is to end up inside it, so these letters are planted within the other pieces rather than laid after them.

blocks.note: co. for company, as in the name over a shopfront
the john and the loo are American and British for the same small room
a rad is a radical, someone at the militant end of a cause

explanation.walkthrough: John Denver reads as one name, and the clue takes it in two: the first half is bathroom slang, and only the second half is defining anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Denver is Colorado's capital, so 'Denver here' asks for the state that city stands in — a place named by what it contains.

clue.text: Ducks once more coming back for rest

indicators.note: Something coming back retraces its path, and in an across entry that means reading the letters from the right.

blocks.note: to duck is to dip, and the re- on the front is 'once more'

explanation.walkthrough: In snooker a spider is the arched rest you stand over the ball for a shot you cannot stretch to, so 'rest' is the table's word and not the sofa's.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider is the long-legged cue rest that arches above a ball in snooker, so 'rest' is being used in its billiard-hall sense.

clue.text: 3 characters in hotel ate ridiculously

indicators.note: Characters are letters, and the ones wanted are those standing inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: eight unbroken letters running across all three words, starting inside the first

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ridiculously' reads as an anagram signal, and that is the trap — it is there to finish the run of letters. The definition is the number, pointing at another entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An elaterid is a click beetle, the family that snaps itself upright when flipped, so it is one instance of what 3 down spells.

clue.text: German band love Foreigner, but not in a nice way

definitions.text: Foreigner, but not in a nice way

blocks.note: the standard single letter, as on a language label
a band is a ring — the thing on a finger, not the group on stage
love is nil in tennis, and nil is written as a nought

explanation.walkthrough: 'German band' and 'Foreigner' build a rock-music surface, and neither has anything to do with the letters: the bands here are a ring and a nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Gringo is what Spanish-speaking Latin America calls an English-speaking outsider, and it is rarely a compliment — which the definition's second half owns up to.

clue.text: Islander’s fine home about to get washed out

blocks.note: fine and OK are the same shrug of approval
somebody at home is in, the way a caller finds them
Chambers lists 'a' as a worn-down form of 'about', which is where a setter finds a spare A
a wan face is pale and drained, washed out

explanation.walkthrough: 'About to get washed out' reads as a weather forecast, and 'about' is really standing on its own. Okinawa is the largest of the islands strung south-west of mainland Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: An Okinawan is a person from Okinawa, so the definition is the plain -an form English builds for the inhabitant of a place.

clue.text: Blue Ivy Carter initially supports Beyonce’s latest nonsense

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of each of those two names is wanted.
A thing that supports sits underneath what it holds up, and in a down entry underneath means further towards the bottom.
The latest of anything is whatever comes last, so this is the final letter of the name in front of it.

blocks.note: the final letter of the singer's name
rot is nonsense — 'what utter rot'
the opening letters of the two names, in the order given

explanation.walkthrough: Blue Ivy Carter is Beyoncé's daughter, so the whole clue reads as one celebrity paragraph — and 'Blue', which looks like the front of the child's name, is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Blue' has meant indecent since the Victorian music hall, the sense that survives in blue jokes and blue films, and that is the register wanted here.

clue.text: Child cuddling cross monster

indicators.note: To cuddle something is to hold it with your arms right round it, which is one word wrapped about another.

blocks.note: in law a minor is a child, anybody under eighteen
the tau cross is the T-shaped one, named for the Greek letter it copies

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' is the trap: it reads as an adjective describing the child's mood, and it is a noun — one particular shape of cross with a Greek name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Minotaur is the bull-headed man kept in the Cretan labyrinth, so 'monster' is the plain category the myth files him under.

clue.text: Console gutted Modigliani over pictures

indicators.note: A gutted building keeps only its shell, so the name here loses everything between its first and last letters.
'over' is turned over: the letters assembled in front of it are then read the opposite way.

blocks.note: Sega built the Mega Drive, so a console can be clued by its maker
M and I are the first and last letters of the painter's name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Console' wants to be a verb about comforting a hard-up painter, which is what makes the surface work. It is the games machine under the television.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a picture in the widest sense — a photograph, a painting, a reflection — so the two words swap in and out of each other freely.

clue.text: Every year songbirds going west over the hill

indicators.note: West is leftwards on the page, so an across answer going west has its letters read from the right.

blocks.note: pa is per annum, the Latin tag printed beside a salary
tits are the small British garden songbirds — blue tits, great tits, coal tits

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is birdwatching, an annual migration heading west, and the definition sits at the end in plain sight, disguised as more scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: To be past it is to be too old to do the thing any more, which is precisely what 'over the hill' says — two idioms for one decline.

clue.text: Long track in evergreen forest

blocks.note: to pine for something is to long for it
ry is the map-maker's short form of railway

explanation.walkthrough: 'Long track' looks like a description of a railway line stretching away. 'Long' is a verb standing on its own, and the track is worth only two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinery is a plantation or wood of pines, and pines keep their needles all year, which is what makes such a wood evergreen.

clue.text: Ground doesn’t vex a Manchester United manager

indicators.note: Ground is the past tense of grind: whatever has been ground is broken up small and comes back in no particular order.

blocks.note: ten letters lifted straight off the clue, ready to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' reads as the stadium, which is what the football surface is for. It is the past tense of grind, and the definition runs from there to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Dave Sexton managed Manchester United from 1977 to 1981, so the definition names him as one holder of the job rather than the only one.

clue.text: Put on endless party

indicators.note: Endless means with its end removed, so the word it applies to arrives one letter short of itself.

blocks.note: to put on a play is to stage it

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a party that never stops, and the instruction is the opposite of that: something has to be cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag is short for a stag party or stag night, the men-only send-off held before a British wedding.

clue.text: The Sun ringing Brockwell for dirt

indicators.note: To ring something is to draw a circle round it, so one piece encloses the other instead of following it.

blocks.note: Sol is the Latin name for the sun; the italics are there to make you read the newspaper instead
a setter in their own clue is I or ME, so the byline is worth one letter

explanation.walkthrough: The italics turn the sun into the tabloid, so the surface is a reporter chasing gossip — 'dirt' in the sense the clue is very happy for you to take.
explanation.definitionFit: Soil is the earth in a garden or a field, and 'dirt' is the everyday word for exactly that; the scandal sense belongs only to the surface.

clue.text: Prime minister’s note opened by billionaire

indicators.note: Something opened by a visitor is split to let them in, so the shorter piece is prised apart and the longer one goes inside.

blocks.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale: doh, ray, mi
Elon Musk is the billionaire everyone knows by the first name alone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like the leaked memo the surface promises. It is a note of music, the sort you sing, and it is only two letters long.
explanation.definitionFit: Giorgia Meloni has led Italy as prime minister since 2022, so the definition names the answer by the office rather than the country.

clue.text: Number 19 nailing 501

indicators.note: To nail something is to fix it in place, and what is fixed in place here is held inside the other word.

blocks.note: 19 down's answer is a synonym for carnal, of the flesh
Roman numerals: D is 500 and I is one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Number 19' reads as a shirt or a front door, and both numbers turn out to be doing something else: one points at another clue, the other is Roman.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardinal number is a counting number — one, two, three — as against an ordinal, so 'Number' names the answer by its own grammatical class.
